# **Comprehensive Technical Review and Reinforcement Learning Integration for the Rotary Inverted Pendulum**

## **Theoretical Modeling, Euler-Lagrange Dynamics, and Parameter Identification**

The Furuta pendulum, or rotary inverted pendulum, is an underactuated mechanical benchmark characterized by two degrees of freedom and a single control actuator1. First introduced by Katsuhisa Furuta and colleagues in 1991 at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, the platform comprises a horizontally rotating base arm driven by an actuator (generalized coordinate ![][image1]) and an unactuated secondary pendulum link (generalized coordinate ![][image2]) that rotates freely in the vertical plane at the tip of the horizontal arm1. The mechanism exhibits severe nonlinearities, state configurations defined on non-Euclidean manifolds (![][image3]), and open-loop instability about its upright equilibrium point1. Although originally developed as a laboratory benchmark, its balancing and stabilization dynamics directly mirror complex engineering systems, including thrust-vector control in rocketry, bipedal humanoid robotic balance, crane cargo anti-sway suppression, and personal balancing transporters1.

The physical assembly couples the actuated horizontal joint to the unactuated vertical pivot, transmitting rotational inertia through centrifugal, Coriolis, and gravitational forces.

## **Classical, Optimal, and Nonlinear Control Syntheses**

Stabilizing an underactuated mechanical plant across its complete operational space requires decomposing the problem into two distinct regimes: large-scale nonlinear energy injection to swing the pendulum up from its hanging resting state, and high-bandwidth linear state feedback to balance it within a localized capture basin around the vertical equilibrium1.  
The control architecture routes sensor feedback through a high-level switching mechanism. When the pendulum rests in the downward hemisphere, the energy-shaping controller commands arm accelerations to pump mechanical energy into the link. Once state trajectories enter the linearized capture basin (![][image96]), supervisory logic transfers authority to a linear balancing controller (such as an LQR or pole-placement state-feedback law) that stabilizes the upright position while regulating arm drift.

### **Energy-Based Swing-Up Control**

Because linear controllers cannot recover the pendulum from the downward equilibrium (![][image97]), swing-up relies on nonlinear energy control, grounded in the foundational formulations developed by Karl Johan Åström and Katsuhisa Furuta10. Neglecting high-order coupling during the initial pump cycles, the instantaneous mechanical energy of the pendulum link, referenced to zero at the upright equilibrium, is expressed as10:  
![][image98]  
where ![][image99] defines the total link inertia about the pivot joint10. At the inverted target state (![][image100]), the target reference energy is ![][image101] (or ![][image102] when referencing potential energy to the lowest hanging configuration)10. Differentiating total energy with respect to time along the system trajectories reveals10:  
![][image103]  
where ![][image104] represents the linear acceleration induced at the pendulum pivot by the base arm10. Selecting a positive-definite Lyapunov candidate based on energy error, ![][image105], its time derivative evaluates to:  
![][image106]  
To guarantee negative semi-definiteness (![][image107]), the base pivot acceleration is commanded to drive the energy error asymptotically to zero10:  
![][image108]  
where ![][image109] is an empirical tuning gain10. Mapping commanded acceleration to motor terminal voltage and introducing control saturation to prevent excessive current draw yields the bounded energy-shaping swing-up law10:  
![][image110]  
Physical implementations often incorporate an auxiliary proportional-derivative feedback term on the base arm angle (![][image1]) to prevent unbounded arm drift during consecutive swing cycles, ensuring the base remains centered within its safe rotational limits5.

### **Linear Balancing Controllers: PID, Pole Placement, and LQR**

Once the swing-up trajectory brings the pendulum within the vicinity of the vertical apex, control is transferred to a linear feedback architecture designed using the linearized state-space model1.  
Dual-loop Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control addresses the underactuated nature of the system by running two parallel control loops into a single actuator voltage command1:  
![][image111]  
The primary inner loop focuses on pendulum balance through high derivative action (![][image112]), which provides the damping needed to stabilize the unstable pole8. The secondary outer loop regulates the horizontal base arm back to its zero setpoint via weak proportional-integral action (![][image113])8. Because the two degrees of freedom are dynamically coupled, tuning these gains requires careful coordination to prevent cross-axis limit cycles and high-frequency chatter14.  
Full-state feedback pole placement synthesizes a state gain matrix ![][image114] such that the closed-loop state matrix ![][image115] exhibits a designer-specified set of eigenvalues ![][image116] in the open left-half complex plane1. Using Ackermann’s formula or the Bass-Gura algorithm, dominant poles are selected to enforce a second-order damping ratio ![][image117] and a 2% settling time ![][image118]1. The remaining poles are placed three to five times further into the left-half plane to ensure fast non-dominant decay without unnecessarily amplifying sensor noise or driving the motor into voltage saturation1.  
The Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) provides an optimal state-feedback gain matrix ![][image119] that minimizes an infinite-horizon quadratic performance index balancing state regulation against control effort1:  
![][image120]  
where ![][image121] penalizes state deviations, and ![][image122] penalizes control effort1. Solving the continuous-time Algebraic Riccati Equation (ARE) yields the unique positive-definite solution matrix ![][image123]6:  
![][image124]  
Weight selection typically follows Bryson’s rule as a baseline, setting diagonal elements to the inverse squares of the maximum acceptable state excursions and actuator limits1:  
![][image125]  
Emphasizing pendulum angular deflection (![][image126]) enforces aggressive disturbance rejection, while tuning ![][image127] prevents the motor from saturating during aggressive recovery maneuvers6. LQR provides guaranteed stability margins under nominal conditions—specifically, infinite gain margin and at least ![][image128] of phase margin—making it a robust foundation for balancing control6.

## **Hybrid Supervisory Architectures and Stateflow Implementation**

Because linear stabilization laws are only valid within a local neighborhood of the upright equilibrium, and energy-based swing-up laws cannot maintain balance at the apex, a hybrid supervisory architecture is required to govern the continuous-time dynamics1. The supervisory controller is modeled as an event-driven finite state machine (FSM) implemented in MATLAB Stateflow, coordinating transitions between continuous-time and discrete-time control laws across three primary operating states1.  
In the SWING\_UP state, the system executes the Åström-Furuta energy shaping law to pump mechanical energy into the pendulum link1. As the link approaches the upright position, the supervisory logic monitors state trajectories until they satisfy a multidimensional entry guard, triggering a transition into the STABILIZE state1. In this balancing state, authority transfers to the linear feedback controller (such as an LQR gain matrix) to balance the pendulum and regulate arm drift1. If an external disturbance knocks the pendulum outside its recoverable envelope, an exit guard triggers an automatic fallback transition back to SWING\_UP1. Finally, an overriding SAFE\_STOP state provides immediate fail-safe shutdown by disabling actuator output whenever hardware limits or thermal safety thresholds are violated1.

Direct switching between continuous controllers can induce severe high-frequency chattering along the boundary of the capture basin, causing violent motor vibrations and rapid loss of balance1. To resolve this, the Stateflow architecture incorporates geometric hysteresis and temporal dwell-time filtering into its transition guards1. The transition from SWING\_UP to STABILIZE requires the pendulum to fall within a tight capture envelope defined by angle, angular rate, and total energy error1:  
![][image134]  
Typical empirical values for physical hardware are ![][image135] (![][image136]), ![][image137], and ![][image138]10. Conversely, the exit transition from STABILIZE back to SWING\_UP is assigned a wider threshold, setting ![][image139] (![][image140])14. This angular separation creates a ![][image141] hysteresis band that prevents limit cycling across the switching boundary14. In addition, the Stateflow chart enforces a temporal dwell-time filter requiring the state trajectory to remain continuously inside the capture basin for at least ![][image142] before committing to the balancing controller14.  
Overriding transitions to SAFE\_STOP protect the hardware by monitoring four continuous safety conditions: horizontal arm overtravel exceeding soft limits (![][image143] on rigs without slip rings), motor overspeed (![][image144]), sustained actuator saturation (![][image145] continuously for over ![][image146] while the motor is stalled), and manual activation of the emergency stop switch1.

Sensor data streams from the physical rig through an asynchronous communications pipeline into a MATLAB App Designer dashboard, which updates strip charts, tracks Stateflow modes, and drives a 3D Simscape Multibody twin to mirror the physical hardware's motion.

### **Simscape Multibody Dynamic Verification**

Simscape Multibody provides a numerical physics engine that simulates the Furuta pendulum without the geometric approximations required by analytical formulations11. Links are modeled as extruded solid bodies defined by two-dimensional planar profiles matched to CAD geometry, allowing the engine to calculate mass, center of gravity, and the full inertia tensor directly from material densities11. Revolute joint blocks connect the bodies, incorporating internal joint stiffness, viscous damping, and Coulomb friction to match the physical pivot bearings11. Actuation torques enter the horizontal joint through a physical signal port interfaced to a DC motor block or dynamic torque controller27.  
Validating this digital twin requires comparing its open-loop trajectory against the analytical ODEs solved in MATLAB using numerical integrators like ode451. Releasing both models from identical non-zero initial conditions confirms that their transient response frequencies and energy decay rates match, verifying the accuracy of the multi-body parameters before closing the control loop1.

### **Real-Time Instrumentation Dashboard**

A dashboard built in MATLAB App Designer provides unified telemetry logging, supervisory mode monitoring, and digital twin synchronization1. Bidirectional communication with the embedded microcontroller runs over a high-speed serial connection (serialport interface) or a low-latency UDP socket at update rates between ![][image147] and ![][image148]1.  
The dashboard interface displays continuous strip charts showing pendulum deflection ![][image149], arm angle ![][image150], and motor voltage ![][image151] alongside real-time indicators that reflect the active Stateflow mode (SWING\_UP, STABILIZE, or SAFE\_STOP)1. As data streams in, the dashboard computes online integral error performance metrics—specifically the Integral of Absolute Error (IAE), Integral of Squared Error (ISE), and Integral of Time-weighted Absolute Error (ITAE)—allowing quantitative performance tracking across disturbance tests1. Simultaneously, the incoming joint coordinates drive an embedded 3D visual canvas or Simulink 3D Animation viewport, rendering a synchronized digital twin that mirrors the physical pendulum's motion in real time1.

Reviewing open-source physical implementations highlights proven approaches for mechanical fabrication, embedded firmware architectures, and low-latency sensor processing pipelines1.  
Embedded firmware architectures require careful coordination between hardware timer peripherals, numerical filtering routines, and discrete control logic1. ### **Embedded Computing Platforms and Velocity Estimation**

Deploying high-gain optimal controllers or high-frequency neural policies imposes strict real-time constraints on embedded microcontrollers1. Platforms such as the STM32 (ARM Cortex-M4/M7) provide dedicated hardware timers with Quadrature Encoder Interface (QEI) peripherals, an integrated hardware Floating Point Unit (FPU), and native support for MATLAB Embedded Coder, making them well-suited for high-bandwidth feedback loops1. Texas Instruments C2000 Delfino microcontrollers (such as the TMS320F28379D) include specialized enhanced Quadrature Encoder Pulse (eQEP) peripherals designed for high-frequency motion control1. Conversely, highly constrained 8-bit boards like the Arduino Nano (ATmega328P) lack hardware floating-point support, requiring distilled neural policies and pre-computed fixed-point arithmetic to maintain loop timing15.  
A primary operational bottleneck on physical hardware is encoder quantization noise8. The unactuated pendulum joint requires high angular resolution (![][image155] quadrature counts per revolution)1. Coarse encoder resolution introduces quantization steps that are magnified by the derivative gains in LQR and PID controllers, generating high-frequency voltage chatter that overheats motor windings8. Furthermore, calculating angular velocities using pure backward finite differences (![][image156]) amplifies high-frequency noise8. Robust firmware implementations filter raw position readings through a first-order low-pass filter with cut-off frequency ![][image157]8, a tracking differentiator, or a steady-state Kalman filter13:  
![][image158]

## **Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Gym Environments, and Sim-to-Real Transfer**

Reinforcement learning formulates the swing-up and balancing problem as a continuous Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple ![][image159]13. Unlike linear controllers that rely on localized operating models, deep reinforcement learning policies can learn end-to-end control laws that handle both swing-up and balance within a single parameterized neural network46.

Physics Engine (MuJoCo / Gymnasium)  
       |  
       |  Continuous Observation: s\_t \= \[cos, sin, angular\_rates\]  
       v  
Neural Actor-Critic Policy (SAC / PPO)  
       |  
       |  Smooth Action: a\_t \= Normalized Voltage / Torque  
       v  
Reward Feedback \+ Action Continuity Regularization  
       |  
       |  Domain Randomization & Latency Buffering  
       v  
TinyML Distillation \-\> Embedded Microcontroller Execution

During simulation training, the physics engine updates system dynamics while domain randomization perturbs parameters and injects transport lag. The neural policy learns a mapping from trigonometric state observations to motor actions, optimizing a continuous reward that balances swing-up progress, balance stability, and actuator smoothness. Once converged, the policy is distilled into a compact neural network for embedded deployment.

### **Observation Manifolds and Reward Engineering**

Because planar rotations wrap around at ![][image160], passing raw angular coordinates directly into a neural network creates artificial discontinuities that destabilize training5. To preserve continuity across the state manifold ![][image3], the observation space maps raw angles to continuous trigonometric projections13:  
![][image161]  
The continuous action space is defined as normalized motor armature voltage ![][image162], scaled internally to physical actuator bounds ![][image163]13.  
Reward function design directly shapes the stability of the learned policy and the smoothness of the resulting control action40. Discontinuous step rewards produce sparse gradient feedback and encourage aggressive bang-bang actuator behavior46. Similarly, pure quadratic penalties create steep gradients near the vertical apex that can lead to divergent policy updates during large swings46. Continuous cosine reward functions, by contrast, provide smooth, well-conditioned gradients across the entire ![][image164] swing profile46. A robust composite reward function incorporates state error, control effort, and action continuity regularization13:  
![][image165]  
The action continuity penalty ![][image166] penalizes high-frequency command oscillations, reducing current spikes and preventing mechanical wear on the physical drive train13.

### **Algorithmic Comparison: PPO vs. SAC vs. DDPG**

The leading model-free reinforcement learning algorithms present distinct trade-offs when applied to underactuated pendulum benchmarks:

* *Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)*: An on-policy actor-critic algorithm that uses a clipped surrogate objective to prevent destabilizing policy updates44. PPO exhibits stable, monotonic policy improvements and low hyperparameter sensitivity, making it resilient to unmodeled disturbances on physical hardware40. However, because it is on-policy, it cannot reuse past experience, requiring large amounts of training data and relying heavily on accelerated parallel physics environments40.  
* *Soft Actor-Critic (SAC)*: An off-policy actor-critic algorithm framed around maximum entropy reinforcement learning49. SAC maximizes both cumulative reward and policy entropy ![][image167], which prevents the policy from prematurely collapsing into suboptimal local limit cycles during swing-up15. Reusing past transitions via an off-policy replay buffer makes SAC an order of magnitude more sample-efficient than PPO, allowing it to fine-tune directly on physical hardware rigs15.  
* *Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG)*: An off-policy actor-critic algorithm using deterministic action selection44. While historically important, DDPG is vulnerable to severe Q-value overestimation bias and brittle hyperparameter tuning in underactuated domains, often lagging behind SAC and PPO in learning stability44.  
* *Hybrid Intelligent Architectures (Fuzzy-LQR / RL-LQR Fusion)*: These architectures combine nominal LQR gains with learned neural policies or fuzzy inference engines21. The analytical LQR guarantees stability within the linear capture basin, while the learned component dynamically compensates for friction, parameter drift, and external impacts21.

### **Sim-to-Real Transfer and Domain Randomization**

Policies trained in idealized simulation environments often fail when deployed directly onto physical hardware due to the reality gap15. This performance gap is driven by unmodeled Coulomb friction, bearing stiction, motor saturation, voltage drops, and transport latency15.  
To enable reliable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, physics environments (such as MuJoCo or Gymnasium) must incorporate systematic domain randomization (DR) and latency modeling during training15. At the start of each training episode, physical parameters are sampled uniformly across randomized distributions15:  
![][image168]  
![][image169]  
In addition, Gaussian white noise is added to simulated states (![][image170], ![][image171]), along with uniform sensor offset biases15. Physical serial interfaces and microcontroller execution introduce control loop latencies between ![][image172] and ![][image173]15. Inserting a FIFO transport delay buffer into the simulation loop trains the policy to anticipate communication lag, preventing latency-induced instability on real hardware15.

### **TinyML and Embedded Policy Distillation**

Deploying deep neural networks onto low-cost microcontrollers requires policy distillation and memory compression15. While training often uses large networks (![][image174] hidden units) to facilitate gradient descent, balancing control can be distilled into compact Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs)15. Ferrolho demonstrated that a minimal network featuring two hidden layers (16 and 8 neurons with ReLU activations), totaling just 689 floating-point parameters, reliably balances a physical rotary pendulum when executed on an 8-bit Arduino Nano15.  
Trained weights and biases are exported as static constant arrays (const float weights\[\]) and compiled into bare-metal C++ firmware15. On 32-bit targets, execution can also leverage the CMSIS-NN acceleration library, ONNX runtime engines, or MATLAB Coder deployment pipelines generated directly from the Reinforcement Learning Toolbox35.

## **Comparative Performance Benchmarks and Engineering Implementation Roadmap**

Selecting an appropriate control architecture requires balancing analytical modeling effort against computational footprint, disturbance rejection, and empirical tracking performance1.

### **Performance Metrics Formulation**

Quantifying controller performance during nominal balancing and external disturbance rejection relies on standard transient and error indices1:

* Peak Overshoot: ![][image175]  
  \[cite: 1, 9\]  
* 10-to-90% Rise Time: ![][image176]  
  \[cite: 1, 9\]  
* 2% Settling Time: ![][image177]  
  \[cite: 1, 9\]  
* Error Integrals:  
  ![][image178]  
  IAE measures cumulative error magnitude, ISE penalizes large transient peaks, and ITAE emphasizes persistent long-term oscillations1.  
* Actuator Effort: Peak voltage (![][image179]) and Root-Mean-Square control effort1:  
  ![][image180]

The following benchmark comparison synthesizes theoretical characteristics and experimental results across classical, optimal, and reinforcement learning paradigms on rotary inverted pendulum hardware1:

| Performance Index / Feature | Dual-Loop PID Control | Full-State Pole Placement | Linear Quadratic Regulator | Hybrid FSM (Swing-Up \+ LQR) | Deep Reinforcement Learning (SAC) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Operational Domain** | Local (![][image181]) | Local (![][image182]) | Local (![][image183]) | Global (![][image164] via FSM) | Global (![][image164] unified) |
| **Rise Time (![][image176])** | Moderate (![][image184]) | Fast (![][image185]) | Fast (![][image186]) | Fast (![][image186]) | Fast (![][image187]) |
| **Settling Time (![][image177], 2%)** | Sluggish (![][image188]) | Moderate (![][image189]) | Short (![][image190]) | Short (![][image190]) | Short (![][image191]) |
| **Peak Overshoot (![][image192])** | High (![][image193]) | Moderate (![][image194]) | Low (![][image195]) | Low (![][image195]) | Moderate (![][image196]) |
| **Disturbance Recovery** | Slow recovery; position drift | Stiff; sensitive to noise | Rapid recovery; well-damped | Rapid recovery; well-damped | Adaptive recovery; broad basins |
| **Control Effort (![][image197])** | High; persistent hunting | Moderate-to-High | Optimal; minimum energy | Optimal during balance | Low-to-Moderate (regularized) |
| **Error Indices (IAE / ITAE)** | High | Moderate | Low | Low | Very Low |
| **Memory Footprint** | Extremely Low (![][image198]) | Low (![][image198]) | Low (![][image198]) | Moderate (![][image199]) | Low in inference (![][image198], TinyML) |
| **Sim-to-Real Vulnerability** | Low (intuitive tuning) | High (model mismatch) | Moderate (stable margins) | Moderate (switching guards) | High (requires Domain Randomization) |

### **Engineering Implementation Roadmap**

Successfully taking a rotary inverted pendulum from mathematical models to a functional physical prototype requires a systematic development process1.  
The development workflow begins with physical parameter identification and digital twin construction1. In this initial stage, link masses and centers of gravity are measured, pivot inertias are determined through bifilar oscillation tests, and joint damping coefficients are extracted from unforced decay logs6. A corresponding multi-body model is assembled in Simscape Multibody using accurate CAD geometries and material densities, and its open-loop behavior is validated against analytical ODE simulations1.  
Once the model is verified, work moves to controller synthesis and numerical validation1. The nonlinear equations of motion are linearized about the upright apex to extract state-space matrices, confirming full system controllability and observability1. Dual-loop PID, pole placement, and LQR balancing controllers are synthesized, using Bryson's rule to configure weighting matrices1. The Åström-Furuta energy-shaping swing-up law is implemented alongside them in Simulink, tuning the energy gain to achieve smooth ascent without over-rotation1.  
Next, the controllers are integrated into a hybrid supervisory architecture for hardware-in-the-loop deployment1. The supervisory state machine is configured in MATLAB Stateflow, incorporating capture basin guards, angular hysteresis deadbands, and fail-safe trip logic1. An instrumentation dashboard is built in MATLAB App Designer to stream real-time telemetry over a serial interface, track supervisory states, compute online error metrics, and synchronize the 3D Simscape digital twin1. Control routines are compiled onto the target microcontroller to validate hardware balancing and benchmark disturbance rejection performance across the classical and optimal controllers1.  
Finally, the project expands into learned control by developing a deep reinforcement learning pipeline1. A custom Gymnasium environment is wrapped around a MuJoCo simulation of the physical platform13. Using Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) or Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), an agent is trained on a continuous cosine reward with action continuity penalties13. Domain randomization across link parameters and transport delay buffers are introduced to bridge the sim-to-real gap15. The trained policy is then distilled into a compact neural network (fewer than 1,000 parameters) and exported as static C++ arrays, enabling bare-metal TinyML execution on the microcontroller to benchmark learned end-to-end control against the hybrid Stateflow/LQR baseline directly on physical hardware15.

## **Conclusion**

The Furuta rotary inverted pendulum is a versatile engineering platform that bridges fundamental classical mechanics, optimal state-space control, hybrid supervisory logic, and modern data-driven reinforcement learning1. While classical dual-loop PID provides an accessible, model-free baseline for balance, its susceptibility to cross-axis coupling and sensor noise limits its performance on coupled underactuated systems8. Full-state feedback pole placement gives direct control over closed-loop dynamics, but requires an accurate system model and can easily saturate physical actuators1. Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR) resolves these limitations by systematically balancing tracking accuracy against actuator effort, offering robust gain and phase margins that make it an ideal choice for localized balance control1.  
Because linear controllers operate within a limited capture basin, practical hardware implementations require a hybrid control architecture1. Pairing an Åström-Furuta energy-shaping swing-up law with a supervisory Stateflow state machine provides reliable global recovery from the hanging position, using angular hysteresis and dwell-time filtering to eliminate boundary chattering and manage hardware safety trips1. Integrating this control stack with a Simscape Multibody digital twin and a real-time App Designer telemetry dashboard establishes a complete Hardware-in-the-Loop workflow that tracks system states, visualizes dynamics, and quantifies performance metrics like IAE and ITAE1.  
Extending the system to deep reinforcement learning demonstrates the viability of learned, end-to-end control on underactuated platforms13. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) can synthesize swing-up and balance behaviors into a single neural network when trained on continuous trigonometric observations and smooth cosine reward functions13. Bridging the reality gap, however, requires systematic domain randomization and transport delay modeling during simulation15. Once trained, policy distillation enables compact neural networks (under 1,000 parameters) to run on low-cost microcontrollers via TinyML, providing a direct comparison between optimal model-based control and learned data-driven policies on physical hardware15.
